ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: Why does a deep neural network need non-linear activation functions between its layers?
options: They make the forward pass faster on GPUs
They keep the weights small so training stays stable
Without them, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear transformation
They are required for backpropagation to compute gradients at all
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Composing linear maps gives another linear map, so without non-linearities extra layers add no expressive power. Backpropagation works fine on purely linear networks; it just can't make them learn non-linear functions.

options: The gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter, using the chain rule and reusing intermediate results
The optimal learning rate for each layer
The final predictions of the network for a batch of inputs
A new random initialisation for weights that performed badly
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Backprop applies the chain rule from the loss backwards through the network, reusing per-layer results so all gradients cost about as much as one forward pass. Predictions come from the forward pass; learning rates are hyperparameters.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: A training run's loss jumps to huge values and then NaN after a few steps. Data and code look correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model has too few parameters
The learning rate is too high, so updates overshoot and diverge
The batch size is too large to fit in memory
The activation function is non-linear
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: An overly large learning rate makes each step overshoot the minimum, growing the loss until values overflow to NaN. A small model underfits but doesn't explode; out-of-memory errors crash instead of producing NaN.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: A very deep network uses sigmoid activations everywhere. The last layers learn, but the early layers barely change. What's going on?
options: The early layers have too many neurons
The loss function is not differentiable
The optimizer skips the early layers to save time
Vanishing gradients: sigmoid derivatives are at most 0.25, so gradients shrink as they're multiplied back through many layers
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Each sigmoid layer multiplies the backward gradient by a derivative of 0.25 or less, so by the early layers it is almost zero. That's why ReLU-family activations, residual connections and normalisation are used. Optimizers update every layer that has a gradient.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: After training with ReLU and a high learning rate, many neurons output 0 for every input and never recover. Why can't they recover?
options: ReLU outputs are capped at 1, so they saturate
Dropout permanently disables those neurons
Their pre-activation is negative for all inputs, so ReLU's gradient is 0 and their weights stop updating
The bias terms are frozen after the first epoch
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: This is the 'dying ReLU' problem: for negative inputs ReLU's gradient is exactly 0, so a neuron stuck in the negative region gets no updates. ReLU has no upper cap; Leaky ReLU and GELU avoid this by keeping a non-zero gradient for negative inputs.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: Why are network weights initialised randomly rather than all set to zero?
options: With identical weights, every neuron in a layer computes the same output and gets the same gradient, so they never become different
Zero weights make the loss function non-differentiable
Random weights guarantee the network starts near the global minimum
Zero weights use more memory than random ones
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Identical initialisation leaves the neurons in a layer symmetric: they compute and update identically, acting like a single neuron. Random init breaks that symmetry. It doesn't place the model near any minimum.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: A teammate says, 'Backpropagation updates the weights.' What's the more precise statement?
options: Backpropagation chooses which layers to freeze; the loss function updates the rest
Backpropagation computes the gradients; an optimizer such as SGD or Adam uses them to update the weights
Backpropagation and gradient descent are two names for the same algorithm
The forward pass updates the weights and backpropagation only checks for errors
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: These are separate steps: backprop works out how the loss changes with each parameter, then the optimizer decides the step, for example w -= lr * grad, or Adam's adaptive update. You can swap optimizers without changing backprop, so they aren't the same algorithm.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: Which of these are hyperparameters you choose, rather than values learned by gradient descent? Select all that apply.
options: Learning rate
Weights of the first layer
Batch size
Number of hidden layers
Bias terms of the output layer
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Learning rate, batch size and depth are set before training, often by tuning. Weights and biases are the parameters that backprop and the optimizer learn. Biases are easy to mistake for configuration, but they are trained like weights.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: Validation loss starts rising while training loss keeps falling. Which actions help with this overfitting? Select all that apply.
options: Add dropout
Keep training for many more epochs
Add weight decay (L2 regularisation)
Stop early at the best validation loss
Make the model much larger without adding data
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: Dropout, weight decay and early stopping all limit how much the model memorises the training set. Training longer makes the gap worse, and a bigger model with no extra data usually overfits more, even though it feels like a fix.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: A single artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies an activation function.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: True. That is the standard neuron: y = f(w·x + b). Layers are many such neurons in parallel, usually implemented as one matrix multiply followed by an element-wise activation.

ai-deep-learning:0.prompt: Backpropagation with gradient descent is guaranteed to find the global minimum of a deep network's loss.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:0.explanation: False. Deep network losses are non-convex, and gradient descent only follows local slopes, so it can settle in local minima or saddle regions. In practice the solutions it finds generalise well enough, but there is no global-optimum guarantee.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: 'How do I reset my password?' and 'I forgot my login credentials' share no keywords, yet a good embedding model places them close together. Why?
options: The model pads both sentences to the same length
The embedding captures meaning learned from data, not word overlap
Both sentences have a similar number of characters
The model stores a dictionary of synonyms and swaps words before comparing
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Embedding models learn from large corpora to map semantically similar text to nearby vectors, so paraphrases with different words end up close. They don't rely on length or a hand-written synonym table.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: An embedding model returns an array of 768 floats whether you send it one word or a whole paragraph. What does 768 represent?
options: The number of tokens the model read
The maximum characters the model accepts
The number of words in its vocabulary
The fixed dimension of the vector space, independent of input length
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Each model outputs vectors of a fixed dimension, so any two outputs can be compared. Input length affects what the vector encodes, not its size. Token limits and vocabulary size are separate properties.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: You indexed documents with embedding model A. Later, queries are embedded with model B, which has the same dimension. Search results become nonsense. Why?
options: Different models produce incompatible vector spaces, so the whole corpus must be re-embedded with the same model
The vector index needs to be rebuilt only because model B is faster
Model B needs a higher similarity threshold to match
Model B's vectors must be normalised before comparison
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Each model learns its own coordinate system, so vectors from different models mean different things even at the same dimension. Normalising or changing thresholds can't align them; re-embed everything with one model.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: The classic word-vector example 'king − man + woman ≈ queen' illustrates what property of embeddings?
options: Embeddings sort words alphabetically
Similar words always have identical vectors
Directions in the space can encode consistent relationships such as gender
Vector arithmetic is how LLMs generate text
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Word2vec-style spaces often encode relationships as roughly consistent offsets, so the man→woman direction also maps king→queen. Similar words are close, not identical, and LLMs don't generate text by this arithmetic.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: A static word embedding (like word2vec) gives 'bank' the same vector in 'river bank' and 'bank account'. Which limitation does this show?
options: Static embeddings cannot represent rare words
One vector per word can't distinguish meanings that depend on context; contextual transformer embeddings can
Static embeddings are too high-dimensional to store
Word vectors only work for English
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Static embeddings assign one vector per vocabulary word, mixing every sense together. Transformer encoders produce contextual embeddings, so each occurrence of 'bank' gets a vector shaped by its surrounding words. Rare words are a separate issue.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: You embed each 30-page document as a single vector. Searches for specific facts buried in those documents perform poorly. What is the main reason?
options: One vector blends the whole document's meaning, diluting specific details
Long documents always produce zero vectors
Vector databases reject large documents
Similarity search only works for documents of the same length
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: One vector has to summarise everything in the document, so a single paragraph's detail barely affects it. Splitting into chunks gives each detail its own vector. Long inputs may also be truncated, but they don't become zero vectors.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: Your embedding model accepts at most 512 tokens. You send 2,000-token documents and notice retrieval never finds facts from the second half of any document. What's the likely cause?
options: The vector index only stores the first half of each vector
Cosine similarity ignores later dimensions
The second half is embedded with a different model
Input beyond the token limit was truncated, so it never influenced the vector
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Many embedding APIs and libraries silently truncate input past the model's limit, or the pipeline cuts it to fit. The cut-off text never affects the vector, which is a strong reason to chunk within the limit. Vector dimensions don't map to positions in the text.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: Which tasks are good fits for text embeddings? Select all that apply.
options: Semantic search over support articles
Clustering customer feedback by topic
Exact arithmetic on numbers in the text
Detecting near-duplicate tickets
Securely hashing passwords
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: Search, clustering and near-duplicate detection all rely on 'similar meaning means nearby vectors'. Embeddings don't do exact arithmetic, and they're not a password hash: they're reversible enough to leak meaning and they aren't salted.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: When storing embeddings in production, what should you keep alongside each vector? Select all that apply.
options: The embedding model name and version
The id of the source document or chunk
The API key used to generate it
The original text or a pointer to it
The IP address of the request that created it
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: The model version tells you when re-embedding is needed and prevents mixing spaces. The source id and text let you show, filter and re-chunk results. API keys must never be stored with data, and request IPs add nothing to retrieval.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: If two different embedding models both output 1,024-dimensional vectors, their embeddings can be compared directly with cosine similarity.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: False. Same dimension doesn't mean same space: each model learns its own coordinate system, so cross-model similarity scores are meaningless. Queries and documents must be embedded by the same model.

ai-deep-learning:1.prompt: Neural text embeddings are typically dense vectors where most dimensions hold non-zero values, unlike sparse bag-of-words vectors.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:1.explanation: True. Dense embeddings spread meaning across all their dimensions. Bag-of-words and TF-IDF vectors are vocabulary-sized and mostly zeros, which is why they work with inverted indexes and BM25.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: Why do modern LLMs use subword tokenization (such as BPE) instead of one token per whole word?
options: It makes every word exactly one token
It removes the need for a vocabulary
A fixed-size vocabulary can still represent rare or new words by composing them from smaller pieces
It guarantees the same token count in every language
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: Subword vocabularies keep common words as single tokens and split rare words like 'unbundling' into known pieces, so there are no out-of-vocabulary words. Whole-word vocabularies either explode in size or fail on new words. Token counts still vary by language.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: For ordinary English prose and typical BPE tokenizers, what is a reasonable rule of thumb for token count?
options: About 4 characters per token, or roughly 3/4 of a word
Exactly one token per word
About one token per character
About one token per sentence
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: English averages about 4 characters, or 0.75 words, per token, so 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words. It's only an estimate: code, numbers and non-English text often need more tokens.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: The same paragraph costs many more tokens in Hindi than in English with the same model. Why?
options: Hindi words are always longer than English words
The API charges extra for non-Latin scripts
Non-English text is translated to English before tokenization
The tokenizer's vocabulary was learned mostly from English, so other scripts break into more, smaller pieces
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: BPE merges are learned from training data frequency. Under-represented scripts get fewer merges and split into more tokens, sometimes individual bytes, which raises cost and uses more context. There's no translation step or language surcharge.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: An LLM often miscounts the letters in a word, for example how many 'r's are in 'strawberry'. What is the main reason?
options: The model was never shown the word during training
The model sees subword tokens, not individual characters, so spelling isn't directly visible to it
Temperature randomness changes the letters
Counting needs more context window than the model has
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: 'strawberry' may be just two or three tokens, and the model has to infer spelling indirectly from those token ids. Character-level tasks are hard for that reason, not because the word is unfamiliar or the context is too short.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: Your Node service estimates tokens as `text.length / 4` to stay under a budget. The budget is regularly exceeded for requests containing JSON and source code. Why?
options: JSON is compressed before it is sent, which changes the length
`text.length` counts bytes, not characters
Code, JSON punctuation, whitespace and identifiers tokenize less efficiently than prose, so the real count is higher; use the model's tokenizer
Token budgets only apply to the model's output
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: The 4-characters-per-token rule is calibrated on English prose. Braces, quotes, indentation and camelCase names split into many tokens. Count with the model's actual tokenizer instead. In JS, `length` counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: You counted a prompt's tokens with one model family's tokenizer and are about to send it to a different family's model. Is the count reliable?
options: No: different model families use different vocabularies, so the same text can produce a noticeably different token count
Yes: tokenization is standardised across providers
Yes, as long as both models have the same context window
Only if the text is pure ASCII
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: Tokenizers are model-specific; vocabulary size and merge rules differ, so counts and ids differ too. Even ASCII text can tokenize differently. Count with the target model's tokenizer, or with the usage numbers the API returns.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: Completions get noticeably worse when your prompt template accidentally ends with a trailing space. What's the most plausible tokenization explanation?
options: Trailing spaces are removed by the API, so the prompt is truncated
Spaces are not part of the vocabulary
The trailing space makes the request exceed the context window
Many BPE tokenizers attach the leading space to the next word's token, so a dangling space forces an unusual token boundary the model rarely saw in training
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: In GPT-style tokenizers ' hello' (with a leading space) and 'hello' are different tokens. Ending with a bare space makes the model continue from an odd boundary, which degrades output. Spaces are definitely in the vocabulary, and one space doesn't overflow the context.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: Which of these consume tokens from a chat model's context window in a request? Select all that apply.
options: The system prompt
Previous conversation turns you resend
Tool or function definitions
Tokens the model generates in its reply
HTTP request headers
Your API key
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: Everything serialised into the model's input (system prompt, history, tool schemas) plus the generated output shares the context window. Headers and the API key are transport and authentication metadata and are never tokenized into the prompt.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: Which statements about byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizers are true? Select all that apply.
options: The vocabulary is built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs in training data
Byte-level BPE can encode any UTF-8 string without an 'unknown' token
The vocabulary is re-learned for each prompt at inference time
A given tokenizer splits the same text the same way every time
Each token always corresponds to exactly one English word
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: BPE learns merges once, offline, from data. Starting from bytes means any input can be encoded, and tokenization is deterministic. It isn't re-learned per prompt, and tokens are often word pieces, punctuation or whole words with a leading space.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: A given piece of text produces the same number of tokens on every LLM provider.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: False. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so counts can differ noticeably for the same text, especially for code and non-English languages. That changes cost comparisons and how much fits in the context.

ai-deep-learning:2.prompt: LLM API pricing and context-window limits are usually expressed in tokens, not characters or words.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:2.explanation: True. Models process tokens, so providers bill per input and output token and state context limits in tokens. Words and characters only give rough estimates.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: What is the main reason transformers replaced RNNs for training large language models?
options: Transformers need no training data
During training, transformers process all positions of a sequence in parallel instead of one step at a time
Transformers use far fewer parameters
RNNs cannot represent words as vectors
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: RNNs carry a hidden state step by step, so training is sequential and long-range signals fade. Attention connects all positions directly and runs in parallel on GPUs, which made training at scale practical. Transformers aren't smaller.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: In scaled dot-product attention, how is a token's output computed?
options: By averaging the embeddings of all tokens equally
By picking the single most similar token and copying it
By running each token through an RNN cell
By scoring its query against every key, softmaxing the scores, and taking the weighted sum of the values
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V: the query–key dot products set how much each other token matters, and the output mixes their value vectors with those weights. It's a soft weighting, not a hard pick or a uniform average.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: Why are attention scores divided by √d_k (the key dimension) before the softmax?
options: Large dot products in high dimensions would push softmax into saturation, where gradients become tiny
To convert the scores into probabilities
To reduce the memory used by the keys
To make attention ignore the first token
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: Dot products grow with dimension. Unscaled, softmax becomes nearly one-hot and its gradients vanish, so scaling keeps training stable. The softmax itself produces the probabilities; the scaling doesn't save memory.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: Why do transformers need positional information (positional encodings or embeddings such as RoPE)?
options: To reduce the vocabulary size
To speed up the softmax
Attention by itself ignores order, so without positions 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look the same
To tell the model which tokens are padding
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: Self-attention treats its input as an unordered set, so shuffling tokens just shuffles the outputs. Adding position information lets the model use word order. Padding is handled by attention masks, not positions.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: How do the compute and memory of standard self-attention grow as the sequence length n increases?
options: Linearly, O(n)
Quadratically, O(n²), because every token attends to every other token
Logarithmically, O(log n)
They don't grow; cost depends only on the model size
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: The attention score matrix is n×n, so doubling the context roughly quadruples attention cost. That's a big reason long contexts are expensive and why efficient-attention variants exist. Model size matters too, but it isn't the whole story.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: What is the purpose of multi-head attention?
options: Several heads attend in parallel in different learned subspaces, so they can capture different kinds of relationships
Each head processes a different user's request
Heads vote and the majority answer is used
It lets the model attend to tokens from future requests
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: Each head has its own Q/K/V projections, so one might track syntax, another coreference, and so on. Their outputs are concatenated and projected, not voted on. Heads have nothing to do with batching users.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: In a decoder-only LLM, what does the causal attention mask do?
options: Hides padding tokens from the loss
Masks out rare tokens to save compute
Stops each position from attending to later positions, so next-token training can't see the answer
Randomly drops attention weights for regularisation
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: During training every position predicts its next token in parallel. The causal mask blocks attention to future tokens so the model can't cheat. Padding masks and dropout are separate mechanisms.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: During generation, inference servers keep a 'KV cache'. What does it store, and what is its main cost?
options: Cached final answers for repeated prompts; costs disk space
The tokenizer vocabulary; costs startup time
Gradients from training; costs GPU memory
Keys and values for tokens already processed, so they aren't recomputed each step; its GPU memory grows with context length
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: Each new token only needs its own Q/K/V. Earlier keys and values are reused from the cache, which makes generation fast, but cache memory scales with sequence length times batch size. It isn't a response cache.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: Which components appear in a standard transformer block? Select all that apply.
options: Multi-head self-attention
A position-wise feed-forward network
Residual connections with layer normalisation
A recurrent hidden state passed between time steps
Max-pooling over the sequence
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: A block is attention plus a feed-forward MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm. Recurrence belongs to RNNs and pooling to CNNs; transformers deliberately avoid recurrence.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: Which statements about encoder-only versus decoder-only transformers are true? Select all that apply.
options: Encoder-only (BERT-style) models use bidirectional attention and suit embeddings and classification
Decoder-only (GPT-style) models use causal attention and suit open-ended generation
Decoder-only models cannot be used for classification
Encoder-only models natively generate long text one token at a time
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: Bidirectional attention gives encoders rich representations for embedding and classification. Causal decoders are built for generation. Decoders can still classify, for example by prompting for a label, and encoders aren't autoregressive generators.

ai-deep-learning:3.prompt: For a given query token, the attention weights over the tokens it attends to sum to 1, because they come from a softmax.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:3.explanation: True. Softmax normalises each query's scores into a probability distribution, so the output is a convex combination of the value vectors. Masked positions simply get weight 0.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: What happens during an LLM's pre-training phase?
options: Self-supervised next-token prediction over a huge corpus of mostly unlabelled text, learning general language and knowledge
Humans rank model answers to teach preferences
The model is trained on a small set of instruction–response pairs
The model is connected to a search engine to learn facts
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: Pre-training is the expensive stage: predict the next token across a very large amount of text, with no human labels needed. Instruction pairs (SFT) and human rankings (RLHF) come later, in much smaller post-training stages.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: You prompt a base model (pre-trained only) with 'What is the capital of France?' and it replies with several more quiz questions. Why?
options: The model doesn't know the answer
The temperature is set too high
A base model just continues text plausibly; it wasn't instruction-tuned to answer questions
Base models can only output code
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: Base models imitate their training text, where a question is often followed by more questions, as in a quiz list. Instruction tuning and preference tuning teach the 'assistant answers the user' behaviour. The fact itself is almost certainly known.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: What is the main purpose of supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) after pre-training?
options: To add up-to-date facts the model never saw
To teach the model to follow instructions and response formats using curated prompt–response examples
To shrink the model so it runs faster
To replace the tokenizer with a better one
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: SFT trains on example conversations so the model learns the assistant role, formats and task behaviour. It isn't a reliable way to inject fresh facts, it doesn't shrink the model, and the tokenizer stays the same.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: In RLHF, what role does the reward model play?
options: It writes the training data for pre-training
It filters toxic content from the pre-training corpus
It decides the learning rate for each step
It's trained on human preference comparisons to score responses, and the LLM is then optimised to maximise that score
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: Humans compare pairs of responses, a reward model learns to predict their preference, and RL (for example PPO) tunes the LLM toward higher reward, usually with a KL penalty to stay close to the original model. It doesn't generate the pre-training data.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: A company wants an assistant that answers from internal docs that change every week, and it must cite its sources. Which approach fits best?
options: Retrieval-augmented generation over the docs, re-indexing as they change
Fine-tune the model on the docs every week
Pre-train a new model from scratch on the docs
Put all the docs in the system prompt once and never update it
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: RAG keeps knowledge outside the weights, so updates mean re-indexing, and every answer can cite the retrieved passages. Fine-tuning is costly to repeat, memorises facts unreliably and can't point to sources. Fine-tuning is better for style and behaviour.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: Why has LoRA become a popular way to fine-tune large models?
options: It retrains every weight but in lower precision
It removes layers to make the model smaller
It freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices, cutting trainable parameters and memory a lot
It only changes the tokenizer, so no GPU is needed
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: LoRA adds low-rank update matrices to selected layers and trains only those, often a tiny fraction of the parameters. Adapters are small, can be swapped per task, and need far less GPU memory. QLoRA adds quantisation, but plain LoRA doesn't retrain all weights.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: After fine-tuning only on medical Q&A, a model got noticeably worse at general coding questions it used to handle well. What is this called?
options: Reward hacking
Catastrophic forgetting
Context overflow
Tokenizer drift
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: Narrow fine-tuning can overwrite general abilities, which is called catastrophic forgetting. Mitigations include mixing in general data, lower learning rates, or parameter-efficient methods like LoRA. Reward hacking is an RL failure mode, not a loss of skills.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: After RLHF, a model writes longer, more confident-sounding answers that score higher with the reward model but aren't more correct. What is this failure mode?
options: Catastrophic forgetting
Underfitting
Data leakage
Reward hacking: the policy exploits weaknesses in the learned reward model
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: The reward model is only an imperfect proxy for human judgement, and optimising hard against it finds shortcuts like length or confident tone. A KL penalty, better reward data and evaluation help. Forgetting is about losing old skills instead.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: Which are good reasons to fine-tune a model instead of only prompting it? Select all that apply.
options: Getting a consistent output format or tone across many requests
Shortening prompts by removing long instructions and examples, which cuts per-request tokens
Teaching a narrow task where you have many labelled examples
Keeping the model current with facts that change daily
Guaranteeing the model never hallucinates
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour: format, tone, task skill. It can also replace long few-shot prompts. It is a poor fit for daily-changing facts, where retrieval works better, and no training method guarantees zero hallucinations.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairs of preferred and rejected responses without training a separate reward model.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: True. DPO optimises the policy directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, skipping the reward model and the RL loop that RLHF with PPO needs. That makes it simpler and more stable to run.

ai-deep-learning:4.prompt: Fine-tuning a model on your documents is the most reliable way to make it cite the exact source of each answer.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:4.explanation: False. Fine-tuning blends documents into the weights and doesn't keep track of where each fact came from, so citations can be invented. RAG passes retrieved passages with ids, so answers can cite and link real sources.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: How does an LLM produce a 100-token response?
options: It generates all 100 tokens in one parallel step
It generates one token at a time, appending each to the input before predicting the next
It retrieves the closest matching response from its training data
It generates the last token first and works backwards
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Generation is autoregressive: predict a distribution, pick a token, append it, repeat. Training runs in parallel over known text, but generation can't, because each token depends on the ones before it. Models don't look up stored responses.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: Why can an LLM state a false fact fluently and confidently?
options: It is trained to produce likely continuations, not verified truths, and has no built-in fact-checking
It deliberately lies when temperature is above 0
Its training data contained only fiction
Its tokenizer corrupts facts
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: The objective rewards text that looks plausible given the context. When knowledge is missing or fuzzy, a plausible-sounding guess is still likely under that objective. That's the root of hallucination; it isn't deliberate deception.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: At each generation step, what does the model itself output?
options: A complete sentence
The single correct next word
An embedding of the whole answer
A score (logit) for every token in the vocabulary, which softmax turns into a probability distribution
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: The final layer produces one logit per vocabulary entry. A decoding strategy such as greedy, temperature or top-p sampling then picks the actual token from that distribution. Choosing the token is a separate step from the model's output.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: Why does an LLM's total response time grow roughly in proportion to the length of its answer?
options: Longer answers are checked for accuracy more times
Output is compressed after generation, which takes longer for long answers
Each output token needs its own sequential forward pass
The API waits a fixed delay between words
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Autoregressive decoding generates tokens one after another, so 500 output tokens take roughly 500 decode steps. The prompt is processed in parallel, but output can't be. That's why limiting output length is a strong latency lever.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: Why does asking a model to reason step by step before giving its final answer often improve accuracy?
options: It raises the model's temperature
The reasoning tokens become context the final answer is conditioned on; answering first commits to a guess
It gives the model access to the internet
It makes the model use a bigger context window
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Each token is predicted from what came before it. Intermediate steps written out first give the answer more relevant context to build on. If the answer comes first, the reasoning can only justify it after the fact. Temperature and tools are unaffected.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: A user asks about a library released after the model's training data was collected. The model describes a plausible but invented API. Why?
options: It has no knowledge of the library past its training cutoff, so it fills the gap with likely-looking text
The library's docs are copyrighted, so the model hides them
The model checked the docs but misread them
The model always invents APIs for JavaScript libraries
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Weights only contain patterns from the training data. For anything newer, the model can only guess by analogy, and guessing looks confident. Supplying current docs in context (retrieval or tools) fixes this. The model didn't read anything.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: How can next-token training be parallelised over a whole sequence even though generation is sequential?
options: The model trains only on the last token of each document
Training uses a separate, non-autoregressive model
Every position predicts its next token at the same time from the true preceding tokens, with a causal mask hiding the future
Sequences are shuffled so order doesn't matter
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: With teacher forcing, the real text is fed in, the causal mask blocks future positions, and the loss is the sum of next-token errors at every position in one pass. Shuffling would destroy the order the model is trying to learn.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: With purely greedy decoding (always taking the most likely token), long outputs sometimes get stuck repeating the same phrase. Why?
options: The KV cache overflows and replays old tokens
The tokenizer runs out of vocabulary
The model is fine-tuned to repeat important points
Always picking the top token can fall into a loop where repeated text keeps making itself the most likely continuation
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Once a phrase repeats, the context makes repeating it again even more likely, and greedy decoding has no randomness to break out. Sampling, repetition or frequency penalties help. Cache overflow and vocabulary exhaustion don't happen this way.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: Which behaviours follow directly from LLMs being next-token predictors? Select all that apply.
options: They can produce fluent but false statements
They struggle with exact arithmetic on long numbers unless given a tool
Their output can change noticeably with small changes to prompt wording
They reproduce their training documents word for word on request
They inherently know today's date
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Predicting plausible tokens explains hallucination, weak digit-level arithmetic and sensitivity to the prompt. Models don't reliably store whole documents verbatim, and they only know the date if it's in the prompt.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: Which statements about chat-style LLM APIs are true? Select all that apply.
options: The messages are serialised into one token sequence using a chat template with special role tokens
The model predicts the assistant's reply tokens given that sequence
By default the model remembers earlier API calls, so you only need to send the newest message
The system prompt is processed by a separate network from the user messages
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: Chat is still next-token prediction over one formatted sequence. Basic chat APIs are stateless: your app must resend the history it wants the model to see. The system prompt is just tokens in the same sequence, often trained to carry more weight.

ai-deep-learning:5.prompt: An LLM answers factual questions by looking them up in a database of facts stored during training.
options: True
False
ai-deep-learning:5.explanation: False. Knowledge is spread across the weights as statistical patterns, and answers are generated token by token. There is no lookup table, which is why recall can be fuzzy or invented. External lookups only happen with retrieval or tools.
